title: Mutual Relations between Elastic Constants
short_intro: Elastic constants define the mechanical response of isotropic linear elastic materials under applied stress systems. The four primary constants—Young's modulus (Y), Bulk modulus (K), Modulus of rigidity (η), and Poisson's ratio (σ)—are mutually interdependent.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct application of standard inter-relations among Y, K, η, and σ, numerical calculations of length and volume changes, and limits of Poisson's ratio.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed tensor-based derivation of inter-relations, strain energy density in terms of elastic constants, and behavior of anisotropic systems.

prerequisites: Definitions of Longitudinal and Shearing Stresses/Strains

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental Elastic Constants
bullets: Young's modulus (Y) is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain within the elastic limit.
Bulk modulus (K) measures the resistance of a material to uniform compression, defined as normal stress to volume strain.
Modulus of rigidity (η) or shear modulus relates tangential stress to shear strain.

concept_notes.heading: Poisson's Ratio (σ)
bullets: Poisson's ratio is the negative ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain under uniaxial tension.
Dimensionless quantity characteristic of the lateral contraction of a stretched rod.
Thermodynamically, for isotropic materials, σ must lie between -1.0 and +0.5.

concept_notes.heading: Independence of Elastic Constants
bullets: For an isotropic solid, only two elastic constants are independent; knowing any two allows determination of the remaining two.
Cross-coupling coefficients link axial loads to transverse deformations via Poisson's ratio.
Dimensional homogeneity requires all elastic moduli to possess the dimensions of pressure [M L&sup{-1} T&sup{-2}].

concept_notes.heading: Limiting Values of Elastic Constants
bullets: Theoretical limits for Poisson's ratio are -1 ≤ σ ≤ 0.5 based on non-negative strain energy.
Incompressible materials (like liquids or rubber-like solids) have a Bulk modulus approaching infinity and σ = 0.5.
Materials with σ = 0 exhibit zero lateral contraction under longitudinal stretch (e.g., cork).

derivations.title: Relation between Y, K, and σ
derivations.conditions: Isotropic material subjected to hydrostatic pressure / uniform triaxial tensile stress
steps: Consider a cube of side 'l' subjected to equal tensile stresses P along the three mutually perpendicular X, Y, and Z axes.
The strain along the X-axis due to stress P along the X-axis is P/Y.
The lateral strains along the X-axis due to stresses P along the Y and Z axes are both -σ(P/Y).
The total net longitudinal strain along the X-axis is ε = (P/Y) - σ(P/Y) - σ(P/Y) = (P/Y)(1 - 2σ).
Bulk modulus K = P / (ΔV/V) = P / [3(P/Y)(1 - 2σ)] = Y / [3(1 - 2σ)].

derivations.title: Relation between Y, η, and σ
derivations.conditions: Isotropic material subjected to pure shear strain
steps: A shearing stress producing an angle θ can be resolved into principal tensile and compressive stresses of magnitude P at right angles.
The tensile stress creates an extension strain of P/Y along one diagonal and a lateral compression strain of σ(P/Y) along the other diagonal.
The total change in length of the diagonal under combined action is proportional to (1 + σ)P/Y.
Equating this strain to half the shear strain θ/2 where θ = P/η yields the relation between shear modulus and Young's modulus.
Simplifying the geometric deformation yields Y = 2η(1 + σ).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stress-Strain Isothermal Compression Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of Hydrostatic Pressure (P) versus Volumetric Strain (ΔV/V). A straight line passing through the origin.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of this linear graph directly gives the Bulk Modulus (K).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to evaluate identification of material compressibility from slopes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's Apparatus Graphical Method
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Load versus Extension graph for a uniform wire.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the linear region gives the ratio of extension to load, used to compute Young's modulus (Y).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct experimental question in practical physics viva and numerical data interpretation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torsional Rigidity Measurement Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Torque (τ) versus Twist Angle (θ) for a cylindrical rod.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope provides the torsional constant, enabling calculation of the modulus of rigidity (η).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions linking geometry of wires to shear modulus variations.

solved_numericals.question: For a given material, the Young's modulus is 1.2 x 10^11 N/m^2 and the Poisson's ratio is 0.25. Find the modulus of rigidity.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Y = 1.2 x 10^11 N/m^2, σ = 0.25.

solved_numericals.question: If the Poisson's ratio of a material is 0.3, find the ratio of Bulk modulus (K) to Modulus of rigidity (η).
solution_steps: Recall expressions for Y in terms of K and σ: Y = 3K(1 - 2σ).
Recall expression for Y in terms of η and σ: Y = 2η(1 + σ).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the Poisson's ratio of a material whose Bulk modulus is equal to its modulus of rigidity.
solution_steps: Use the formula for Poisson's ratio in terms of K and η: σ = (3K - 2η) / (6K + 2η).

assumptions_and_limitations: Materials are assumed to be perfectly homogeneous and isotropic.
Deformations are strictly within the elastic limit obeying Hooke's law linearly.
Temperature remains constant (isothermal conditions), as elastic constants vary with temperature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Poisson's ratio can have any positive or negative value without restriction.
common_misconceptions.correct: Poisson's ratio for isotropic solids must lie strictly between -1 and +0.5.
common_misconceptions.why: Values outside this range violate thermodynamic stability requirements regarding positive strain energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An isotropic material has four independent elastic constants.
common_misconceptions.correct: An isotropic material has only two independent elastic constants.
common_misconceptions.why: All four constants (Y, K, η, σ) are interlinked; knowing any two determines the other two.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Bulk modulus represents deformation in a single linear direction.
common_misconceptions.correct: Bulk modulus represents uniform volumetric deformation under isotropic hydrostatic pressure.
common_misconceptions.why: It involves simultaneous compressive stresses along all three mutually perpendicular axes.

quick_revision: Only two elastic constants are independent for isotropic solids
